card_summary: The recent AWS announcement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a clear indication that the industry is moving towards more sophisticated media supply chain automation. This, in turn, will drive the adoption of standards-based, IP-centric architectures, particularly ST 2110, which has been gaining traction in live production environments. As a result, we can expect to see more widespread use of NMOS for device discovery and control, as well as RIST for low-latency, high-quality video transport over IP networks. In practice, this means that engineering teams will need to carefully manage signal integrity and latency across the entire production chain, from camera to playout. The use of standards like ST 2110 and AES67 will help ensure frame-accuracy and low-latency transport, but will also introduce new challenges related to genlock and clock synchronization. To mitigate these risks, engineers will need to implement robust clock management and genlock systems, such as those provided by 12G-SDI and JPEG XS, to ensure that signals remain synchronized and intact throughout the production process.

Why Broadcasters Must Rethink Signal Transport for Real-Time OTT Delivery

Live signal transport is at a crossroads. The shift to real-time OTT delivery has created a perfect storm of latency, signal integrity, and frame-accuracy concerns. Broadcasters are no longer just transmitting to a handful of regional audiences; they're now streaming to a global audience that expects instant gratification. The pressure to deliver high-quality, low-latency content is mounting, and the traditional broadcast infrastructure is struggling to keep up.

What This Development Actually Means

AWS has announced the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a software-based solution that enables intelligent media supply chain automation. This means that broadcasters can now leverage cloud-based processing and analytics to streamline their signal transport workflows, reducing latency and improving signal integrity.

This development sits within the broader context of the industry's shift towards cloud-native production and OTT delivery. The increasing demand for real-time streaming has created a perfect storm of technical challenges that traditional broadcast infrastructure is struggling to address.

Why It Matters for Broadcast Operations

The introduction of cloud-based signal transport and automation will have significant implications for broadcast operations. One of the most pressing concerns is the need to reduce latency and improve signal integrity. This will require broadcasters to reassess their infrastructure and consider the adoption of new technologies such as ST 2110, NDI, and SRT. For example, Matrox ConvertIP gateways are already being used to transport high-quality, low-latency signals over IP networks, while Riedel MediorNet is providing real-time signal routing and switching capabilities. Meanwhile, Harmonic VOS360 and Telestream Vantage are offering advanced encoding and transcoding capabilities that can help reduce latency and improve signal quality.

Impact by Stakeholder

  • Regional and national broadcasters: Will need to budget for the upgrade of their infrastructure to support cloud-based signal transport and automation. This will involve the adoption of new technologies such as ST 2110 and NDI, as well as the integration of cloud-based processing and analytics. By doing so, they can reduce latency and improve signal integrity, enabling them to deliver high-quality, low-latency content to their audiences.
  • OTT and streaming platforms: Will need to adapt their content delivery networks (CDNs) to support the increased demand for real-time streaming. This will involve the adoption of new technologies such as ABR ladders and SSAI, as well as the integration of cloud-based processing and analytics.
